### Live Synthesis | GridPulse Scotland

Scottish generation nodes are currently delivering a robust 4.4 GW of wind output, suppressing regional grid carbon intensity to a clean 32 gCO2/kWh. However, this northern generation surplus starkly illustrates the enduring physical limitations of Great Britain’s transmission architecture. The Cheviot boundary (B6) is operating at near-capacity, severely restricting bulk power transfers southward into England’s primary demand centers.

To maintain dynamic system stability, the Electricity System Operator (ESO) must aggressively intervene. With 221.1 MWh of wind generation already curtailed within this settlement window, zero-marginal-cost clean electrons in the north are actively turned down, while synchronized fossil-fueled generation is constrained on south of the boundary to meet unmet demand. 

This localized saturation delivers significant economic headwinds. The twin costs of compensating curtailed northern wind farms and dispatching expensive, out-of-merit downstream generation directly inflate Balancing Services Use of System (BSUoS) charges. Until major inter-regional subsea links and high-voltage transmission reinforcements across the Anglo-Scottish border are commissioned, high-yield generation events will continue to present this operational paradox: exceptional green output decoupled from southern load, resulting in stranded energy and heightened systemic costs borne by consumers.
